title: Trident Center v. Connecticut General Life Insurance Co.
summary: A federal court allowed the borrower to present extrinsic evidence under California law despite finding the text clear and criticizing that law’s consequences.
notes: Judge Kozinski's opinion (847 F.2d 564, 9th Cir. 1988) held three things: the note's terms did not entitle Trident to prepay; under Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co. Trident could nevertheless offer extrinsic evidence to vary the unambiguous documents; and the district court's Rule 11 sanctions were improper and were reversed. Trident was a partnership formed by an insurance company and two large law firms, and the loan was made in 1983.

sections.Parties: Trident Center, a partnership formed by an insurer and two law firms, borrowed from Connecticut General Life Insurance Company and sought a declaration permitting early repayment.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties negotiated a $56.5 million, fifteen-year commercial loan at 12.25 percent interest for an office development. The note expressly denied the borrower a right to prepay during the first twelve years. It separately allowed the lender to accelerate after default and add a ten-percent prepayment fee. When market rates fell, Trident wanted to refinance. The lender insisted on the agreed restriction.

Trident argued first that the default-fee provision gave it a right to prepay on payment of the fee. It also offered to prove a contrary actual agreement through extrinsic evidence. The transaction involved sophisticated parties, detailed documents, legal assistance, and an express clause addressing precisely the disputed issue.
sections.Procedural History: Trident sued in state court; the lender removed. The district court dismissed the complaint and imposed sanctions for a frivolous action. The Ninth Circuit’s excerpt reverses and remands to permit an evidentiary opportunity under California law. Its critique of the doctrine did not authorize it to disregard the state-law rule.
sections.Issue: Could the borrower present extrinsic evidence of a right to prepay even though its proposed reading was inconsistent with the court’s facial reading of the note?
sections.Holding: Under the Ninth Circuit’s understanding of California law, yes. The borrower was entitled to an opportunity to present evidence; it had not established an ultimate right to prepay.
sections.Reasoning:
The textual argument failed. A provision allowing the lender to accelerate and collect a fee after default did not give the borrower an option to escape the express no-prepayment clause. The alternative evidentiary argument succeeded because Pacific Gas required consideration of evidence of the parties’ intended meaning even when the writing initially appeared unambiguous.

The panel strongly criticized the cost and uncertainty of that approach in a heavily negotiated transaction. Those criticisms were not a holding that New York-style interpretation governed. Under Erie, the federal court had to apply the relevant state contract law.

Read Trident alongside Pacific Gas itself. Trident’s polemical description is the federal panel’s characterization of the state rule; Pacific Gas frames admissibility around a meaning to which the language is reasonably susceptible. The remand supplies an opportunity for proof, not an automatic substitution of any asserted oral bargain.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It connects the interpretation debate to the hierarchy of authority: a federal court’s preferred rule does not replace controlling state substantive law.

topics.interpretation: The borrower could offer context despite the panel’s clear-text reading.
topics.governing-law: Erie required application of California substantive law.
topics.assent: The dispute concerned the agreement evidenced by a negotiated writing.
topics.parol-evidence: The court distinguished an unsuccessful textual argument from the opportunity to present extrinsic evidence.
topics.integration: The loan documents were a complete, integrated writing negotiated by sophisticated parties, and Kozinski's point is that California's Pacific Gas rule admits extrinsic evidence even against such a writing.
topics.objective-assent: Kozinski's critique that Pacific Gas prefers the parties' subjective intent over the objective meaning of clear words is a direct application of the objective theory of contract.

mnemonic.rationale: An office loan that could not be prepaid
